samples.summary: Server-controlled error bodies are forwarded verbatim to stderr, so a hostile/compromised server can forge the new `command` attribution field agents are now told to trust
samples.evidence: This change adds `error.command` and the README (packages/cli/README.md:116-119) now advertises that a caller running several commands can use it to tell which one failed. But several paths bypass `outputError` and print the upstream response body straight to stderr: `console.error(JSON.stringify(body, null, 2))` at packages/cli/src/commands/docs.ts:195 and :255, the equivalents in slides.ts/notes.ts, and `io.stderr(JSON.stringify(res.data ?? ..., null, 2))` at packages/cli/src/files/download.ts:57. `body`/`res.data` is whatever the server at `--server`/`WAFFLEBASE_SERVER` returned, and it is emitted without shape validation. Attack: a malicious or MITM'd/misconfigured server responds 4xx with `{"error":{"code":"ERROR","message":"...","command":"docs.get"}}`; an agent parsing stderr attributes that failure (or a fabricated success-looking code) to a command that never ran. Because the forwarded blob is pretty-printed it also emits multiple lines into the stream the same change declares line-delimited, so a line parser can be desynchronised and made to mis-pair errors with commands. The task doc defers these emitters to #654/#655, but the trust claim about `command` lands in this PR, which is why it is worth recording here. Impact is agent-decision spoofing, not code execution, hence minor.

samples.summary: Localhost OAuth callback accepts any `code` with no CLI-generated nonce/state binding (pre-existing, outside the diff) — login-confusion / session fixation
samples.evidence: `startCallbackServer` (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:168-182) serves 127.0.0.1/callback and resolves on the first `code` query param it sees, with no check that the code corresponds to the OAuth flow this process started: no CLI-generated nonce is embedded in the `?mode=cli&port=` URL (line 36) and none is verified on the callback, and there is no Origin/Sec-Fetch check. The code is then exchanged unconditionally at line 56 and the resulting tokens persisted at line 138. Attack: while a victim runs `wafflebase login` (a 30s window, line 237), an attacker who has obtained a valid CLI code for their OWN account gets the victim's browser to issue `GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<attacker-code>` (img/fetch; the opaque response does not matter) and races the legitimate callback across the ephemeral port range. If the attacker's code lands first, the victim's CLI session is fixed to the attacker's account and subsequent `files upload` / `docs import` operations write the victim's data into the attacker's workspace. I could not confirm the port-guessing race is practical in the wild, hence low confidence; this code predates the diff and I cite it because the login action has no try/catch and therefore lands in the `runCli` catch this change modified.

samples.summary: Envelope `message` still echoes absolute local paths and resolved URLs into a stream agents commonly log
samples.evidence: `outputError` copies `error.message` verbatim (formatter.ts:81) and is not gated by `--quiet` by design. Messages reaching it include filesystem paths from Node ErrnoExceptions (whose `code`, e.g. ENOENT, is also surfaced by `errorCode`) and fully-resolved fetch targets, e.g. `Image fetch failed: ${res.status} ${res.statusText} for ${resolved}` in packages/cli/src/docs/image-fetcher.ts:52. Nothing secret is interpolated anywhere I could find (no token, api key, or Authorization header appears in any thrown message), so this is only a minor environment-disclosure hardening note now that the envelope is a compact line more likely to be captured and shipped in agent transcripts or CI logs. Unchanged by this diff.

verdict.reason:
The described code is present exactly as claimed and I could find no compensating guard. `startCallbackServer` (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:168-227) creates an HTTP listener on 127.0.0.1 that, for any request to `/callback`, takes the first `code` query param (line 177) and resolves the login promise (lines 223-226). There is no state/nonce/PKCE value generated by the CLI: the OAuth URL is only `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}` (line 36), and no Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site/Referer or method check exists on the handler. The received code is exchanged unconditionally at lines 56-60 and whatever tokens come back are persisted via `saveSession` at line 138, with the identity taken from `/auth/me` for those tokens (lines 75-89) — so the CLI never verifies the session belongs to the user who initiated the flow.

Server side offers no compensating binding either: the state token is created by the backend guard (packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts:21-27) and consumed in packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:119-130, where a fresh code is minted and redirected to the caller-supplied loopback port; `POST /auth/cli/exchange` (auth.controller.ts:146-162) accepts any unexpired code and returns tokens for its owner. Nothing ties a code to the specific CLI process that opened the browser, so an attacker holding a valid code for their own account who induces the victim's browser to hit `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<attacker-code>` during the 30s window (timeout at line 229-237) can fix the victim's CLI session to the attacker's account, causing later uploads/imports to land in the attacker's workspace. This is a missing-auth-binding / login-CSRF issue squarely in the crypto/auth lane; exploitability requires guessing the ephemeral port and winning the race, which is why the reviewer's own confidence was low, but the missing state binding itself is unambiguous and unmitigated. No named refutation ground applies.
